title: Using Modeled Subsurface Ocean Temperature Hindcasts in Fisheries Science Applications
content:
ABSTRACT

Fisheries research often incorporates sparsely observed characteristics of the ocean such as subsurface temperature into analyses. This requires output from numerical ocean models and validation to ensure accuracy and precision at desired spatial and temporal scales. The goal of this study was to pair in situ subsurface temperature observations with an off-the-shelf model-based subsurface temperature product, evaluate potential improvements through the addition of spatial and temporal covariates, and assess modeled temperature accuracy and precision for Alaska fisheries science applications. Temperature-depth profiles collected during three fishery-independent surveys occurring in three large marine ecosystems of Alaska (the Eastern Bering Sea, Aleutian Islands, and Gulf of Alaska) were used to evaluate the skill of subsurface temperature hindcasts from a global ocean model, the Hybrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM). Spatially blocked 10-fold cross-validation was used to select bias-corrected hindcasts that included HYCOM output with additional covariates to explain temperature differences. Although HYCOM reasonably simulated vertical, spatial, seasonal (May–September), and interannual temperature patterns, its hindcasts showed biases and imprecision that were improved with bias-correction models. Three case studies compared the utility of using HYCOM versus bias-correction model hindcasts of subsurface temperature: a daily bottom temperature index in the Gulf of Alaska, Bering Sea cold pool metrics, and Pacific cod geolocation models. In a large and sparsely sampled region like Alaska, combining multiple datasets of subsurface temperature observations provided a useful way to assess model output before use in fisheries research.
